title: Bath soap: melt-and-pour and a 5% superfat bar

say: Welcome to Bath Soap Production, module 3 of our soap making course.
A bath bar touches skin every day, so this module is about balance. We'll make a quick melt-and-pour bar, then a cold-process bath bar at 5% superfat.

shots.label: Melt-and-pour soap base
say: These cubes are melt-and-pour base, soap a factory has already made. There is no caustic soda to handle.
The trade-off is cost. Each bar costs more, so use it for gifts, samples and quick orders.

shots.banner: Keep rubbing alcohol away from flames
say: Melt the cubes gently, in a bowl over hot water, and never let it boil. Overheated base turns thick and rubbery.
Off the heat, stir in colour, then fragrance at the supplier's rate, and pour.
A light spray of isopropyl alcohol pops the bubbles. It is highly flammable, so never spray it near a gas flame.
Wrap each bar in cling film as soon as you unmould it. In humid places like Lagos, unwrapped bars soon look wet and beaded.

shots.label: Palm, olive, PKO, shea, castor
say: Now the main bath line, cold process. Instead of copying a recipe, you design one with the quality numbers in SoapCalc.
For a bath bar, keep cleansing between 12 and 22. In practice, keep PKO or coconut oil to about a fifth of the oils, and let palm oil, shea and olive carry the rest.
Here is Zainab's formula from Abuja, weighed out in grams for 2,000 g of oils. Copy this card.
Each oil goes on the scale separately, and each weight is ticked on the sheet.
At 5% superfat she needs 275 g of pure caustic soda. Her flakes are 99% pure, so she weighs 278 g.
The water is 558 g. At 2% superfat she would need about 284 g, so her 5% choice gives a milder bar.

shots.label: Caustic soda (sodium hydroxide)
say: These white, dry flakes are the caustic soda. Even a small batch needs full care.
Keep the tub sealed, because damp flakes lose strength.

shots.label: Goggles, gloves, long sleeves
say: Before you open it: sealed goggles, long gloves over your wrists, long sleeves and an apron.
Keep a running tap or a big container of clean water within reach.

shots.label: Caustic soda INTO water
shots.banner: Never pour water onto caustic soda
say: Outdoors, watch: the flakes go slowly into the cold water, a little at a time, while we stir.
Never pour water onto caustic soda. Step back from the heat and fumes, then let the solution cool.
Melt the palm oil, PKO and shea, then add the olive and castor oil, which cools the mix.
Many makers combine when the oils and lye solution are both warm, not hot, below about 45 degrees Celsius.

shots.label: Light trace
say: Pour the lye into the oils, then stick blend in short bursts, stirring between, until light trace. A drizzle just leaves a trail.
Add fragrance now. Some fragrance oils make the batch thicken suddenly, so test new ones in a small batch first.
Pour into a lined mould, tap out the air, cover it, and wrap it in an old towel for 24 hours so it heats evenly.
But if your batch has honey, which adds heat, don't wrap it. Leave it in a cool room so the top doesn't crack.
Unmould and cut after one to two days, wearing gloves, because fresh soap is still caustic.
Cold-process bath bars must cure for 4 to 6 weeks on racks, in a shaded, airy room, out of children's reach.
The bar becomes harder, milder and longer-lasting. Do a pH strip test before you sell.

shots.label: Kaolin, honey, fragrance
say: Additives start small: about 1 teaspoon of kaolin clay or honey per 500 g of oils. Fragrance is weighed from the oils, so 2% of 2,000 g is 40 g, never above the supplier's maximum.
Never add mercury or skin-bleaching chemicals. And make cosmetic claims only, like gentle cleansing with shea butter, never cures eczema.
Well done. Now go through the lessons below, and do the practice task: enter Zainab's formula in SoapCalc, then make a small test batch.
